source: Yeo et al. 2011 (resting-state intrinsic networks, 7-network parcellation), Thomas Yeo 17

networks.name: Visual network
networks.summary: Primary and extrastriate visual cortex plus the lateral geniculate relay: calcarine/lingual/occipital gyri, cuneus, and the occipital pole.
function: Early (V1–V3) and extrastriate (hV4, lateral occipital complex) processing of retinotopic input.
Feeds the dorsal ('where'/action) and ventral ('what'/perception) visual streams.
states: Active during passive and active visual perception, including low-level feature detection and visual imagery of scenes and objects.
paradigms: Retinotopic mapping with flickering checkerboards and rotating wedges / expanding rings (Engel et al. 1994).
Passive movie viewing and object/scene recognition in task-based fMRI.
tracts: Optic radiation (lateral geniculate nucleus → primary visual cortex)
Inferior longitudinal fasciculus (occipital → ventral temporal cortex)
Optic tract and optic nerve (retinal → LGN relay)

disorders.note: Bilateral V1 damage abolishes conscious vision; anosognosia for the deficit is characteristic.
Ventral-stream lesions impair object recognition despite spared low-level vision.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Engel SA, Rumelhart DE, Wandell BA, et al. (1994) fMRI of human visual cortex. Nature 369:525.

networks.name: Somatomotor network
networks.summary: Primary motor and somatosensory cortex with the supplementary motor area: precentral/postcentral and paracentral gyri.

nodeNotes.Precentral sulcus (Superior part): supplementary motor area (shared with the frontal eye fields of the dorsal attention network)

function: Primary motor (M1) and primary somatosensory (S1) cortex, with the supplementary motor area (SMA), mediating voluntary movement execution and somatosensation.
states: Active during overt and imagined movement; somatotopically organized as the motor and sensory homunculi.
paradigms: Finger/hand movement tasks contrasted with rest; vibrotactile stimulation to map digit somatotopy (Penfield & Boldrey 1937).
tracts: Superior thalamic radiation (ventral posterolateral nucleus → S1)

disorders.note: M1/corticospinal lesions produce spasticity, hyperreflexia, and weakness.
S1 damage impairs tactile discrimination and object recognition by touch.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Penfield W, Boldrey E (1937) Somatic motor and sensory representation in the cerebral cortex of man as studied by electrical stimulation. Brain 60:389–443.

networks.name: Dorsal attention network
networks.summary: Goal-directed (top-down) attention: intraparietal sulcus, superior parietal lobule, and the frontal eye fields.

nodeNotes.Precentral sulcus (Superior part): frontal eye fields (shared with the supplementary motor area)

function: Goal-directed (top-down) allocation of spatial attention and eye-movement planning; encodes attended spatial locations.
states: Active during sustained spatial attention and saccade preparation/execution; deactivated during mind-wandering.
paradigms: Posner spatial-cueing tasks, saccade and visual-search paradigms, and covert attention to peripheral targets (Corbetta & Shulman 2002).
tracts: Frontal aslant tract (supplementary motor / frontal eye field region)

disorders.note: Right-hemisphere DAN lesions (parietal or frontal eye fields) cause contralesional neglect.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Corbetta M, Shulman GL (2002) Control of goal-directed and stimulus-driven attention in the brain. Nat Rev Neurosci 3:201–215.

networks.name: Ventral attention / salience network
networks.summary: Stimulus-driven reorienting and salience detection: temporoparietal junction, ventral frontal cortex, and anterior insula.

nodeNotes.Superior temporal gyrus (Lateral part): posterior superior temporal gyrus — temporoparietal junction
nodeNotes.Angular gyrus: ventral/anterior part at the temporoparietal junction

function: Stimulus-driven reorienting of attention to salient or unexpected stimuli; detection of behaviorally relevant events.
Integrates interoceptive and limbic signals (the 'salience' component anchored in the anterior insula).
states: Transiently active at stimulus onset / oddball detection; tonically modulates switching between the default-mode and executive networks.
paradigms: Auditory and visual oddball detection, stop-signal tasks, and salience/novelty paradigms (Seeley et al. 2007).
tracts: Fronto-insular white matter (anterior insula → inferior frontal cortex)

disorders.note: Dysregulated salience attribution is linked to delusions and hallucinations.
Anterior insula dysfunction associates with altered bodily-signal processing.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Seeley WW, Menon V, Schatzberg AF, et al. (2007) Dissociable intrinsic connectivity networks for salience processing and executive control. J Neurosci 27:2349–2356.
Corbetta M, Shulman GL (2002) Control of goal-directed and stimulus-driven attention in the brain. Nat Rev Neurosci 3:201–215.

networks.name: Limbic network
networks.summary: Emotion and memory: temporal pole, orbitofrontal cortex, subgenual anterior cingulate, hippocampus/parahippocampus, and the amygdala.

nodeNotes.Hippocampus: anterior hippocampus (emotional memory; shared with the default mode network)

function: Emotion, motivation, and memory encoding, integrating olfactory, visceral, and mnemonic signals via the amygdala, hippocampus, and orbitofrontal cortex.
states: Active during emotional experience and recall; tonically active at rest as part of the 'emotional' component of the default system.
paradigms: Emotional face and picture viewing, autobiographical/emotional memory recall, and olfactory stimulation.

disorders.note: Amygdala–orbitofrontal dysregulation underlies pathological anxiety and depression.
Hippocampal/amygdala involvement can produce emotional and memory symptoms.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Catani M, Dell'Acqua F, Thiebaut de Schotten M (2013) A revised limbic system model for memory, emotion and behaviour. Neurosci Biobehav Rev 37:1724–1737.
Pessoa L (2017) A network model of the emotional brain. Trends Cogn Sci 21:357–371.

networks.name: Frontoparietal control network
networks.summary: Flexible cognitive control: dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior inferior parietal lobule, and lateral precuneus.

nodeNotes.Supramarginal gyrus: anterior part — anterior inferior parietal lobule

function: Flexible, goal-directed cognitive control: working memory, task switching, planning, and top-down regulation of other networks.
states: Active during effortful cognitive tasks; flexibly couples with the default-mode (introspection) or dorsal-attention (external focus) network depending on task demands.
paradigms: N-back working memory, task-switching, Stroop, and planning (Tower of London) tasks (Cole et al. 2013).
tracts: Superior longitudinal fasciculus II/III (frontoparietal control circuit)

disorders.note: ADHD, traumatic brain injury, and schizophrenia associate with frontoparietal hypoconnectivity and impaired control.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Cole MW, Reynolds JR, Power JD, et al. (2013) Multi-task connectivity reveals flexible hubs for adaptive task control. Nat Neurosci 16:1348–1355.
Dosenbach NUF, Fair DA, Miezin FM, et al. (2007) Distinct brain networks for adaptive and stable task control in humans. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 104:11073–11078.

networks.name: Default mode network
networks.summary: Internally-directed cognition: posterior cingulate/precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex, angular gyrus, and medial temporal lobe.

nodeNotes.Superior frontal gyrus: medial superior frontal gyrus (medial prefrontal cortex)
nodeNotes.Cingulate gyrus and sulcus (Middle anter: anterior cingulate cortex (shared with the limbic network)
nodeNotes.Straight gyrus (Gyrus rectus): medial prefrontal cortex (shared with the limbic network)

function: Internally-directed cognition: autobiographical memory, self-referential thought, future simulation, and social cognition.
states: Most active at rest and deactivates during externally-focused tasks; supports mind-wandering and mental time travel.
paradigms: Resting-state vs. task contrast, autobiographical memory recall, self-referential trait judgement, and future thinking (Buckner et al. 2008).
tracts: Cingulum bundle (posterior cingulate ↔ medial prefrontal; not discretely modeled in this atlas)

disorders.note: Posterior cingulate/precuneus shows early hypometabolism and amyloid deposition.
Medial prefrontal–posterior cingulate hyperconnectivity is a robust finding.
Reduced DMN deactivation during externally-focused tasks.

citations.source: Yeo BTT, Krienen FM, Sepulcre J, et al. (2011) The organization of the human cerebral cortex estimated by intrinsic functional connectivity. J Neurophysiol 106:1125–1165.
Buckner RL, Andrews-Hanna JR, Schacter DL (2008) The brain's default network: anatomy, function, and relevance to disease. Ann N Y Acad Sci 1124:1–38.
Raichle ME, MacLeod AM, Snyder AZ, et al. (2001) A default mode of brain function. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 98:676–682.
